description: Constructs the ADS business conditions index: a dynamic-factor framework measuring real activity at high frequency from mixed-frequency stock and flow indicators, updated in real time as components are released or revised, an explicitly real-time, vintage-aware measurement methodology.

BEA reliability study assessing GDP/GDI accuracy via the magnitudes and patterns of NIPA revisions rather than against an unknown true value; documents the vintage sequence (advance, second, third, annual, comprehensive) and the reasons for revision (replacement of extrapolations with fuller source data, definitional/comprehensive changes).

Analyzes the GDP-GDI statistical discrepancy: even after annual and benchmark revisions, GDP (expenditure-based) and GDI (income-based) differ because of source-data differences, concept/definition adjustments, interpolation/extrapolation methods, and timing of quarterly seasonal adjustment; the discrepancy persists but GDP and GDI levels share the same trend and rarely diverge far.

Establishes vintage estimates as repeated estimates of the same quarter, so early estimates carry quantifiable uncertainty; assesses accuracy by revision magnitudes/patterns (not against a true value). Of a ~2% average current-dollar GDP revision, about one-third stems from concept/definition changes and two-thirds from statistical revisions.

Survey of Professional Forecasters documentation (Philadelphia Fed): quarterly survey begun 1968Q4 (ASA/NBER), taken over by the Phila Fed 1990Q2; documents survey/variable history including long-term (10-year) projections added 1992Q1 and other variable additions (1981Q3), defining a real-time forecast dataset whose composition has changed across vintages.

Phila Fed methodology note for the ADS index: index updates in real time as new OR revised component data are released by BEA, BLS, Census, DOL and FRB; documents index components, data transformations, and the release-timing dependence that makes the index itself revise with each data vintage.

Pozsar, Adrian, Ashcraft & Boesky (FRBNY Staff Report) map the US shadow-banking system - credit intermediation by nonbank entities outside the regulated perimeter and outside conventional monetary/flow-of-funds measurement - documenting its scale and pre-crisis growth. Commentary identifying a shadow-banking measurement and monitoring gap.

Pozsar (OFR) advances a money-view taxonomy of shadow-bank money claims (Par-on-Demand / Par-at-Maturity tiers) and argues the official monetary aggregates (M0/M1/M2) and the Financial Accounts of the United States (formerly the Flow of Funds) inadequately capture short-term wholesale funding and dealer-bank intermediation. Commentary on a monetary-aggregate / flow-of-funds measurement gap for shadow money.

Fixler, Gindelsky & Johnson describe BEA new Distribution of Personal Income measure (built from public microdata for 2007-2016) and note that methodological choices such as the treatment of the 1986 Tax Reform Act drive divergence between PSZ and Auten-Splinter tax-based results. Commentary on NIPA-based vs tax-based distributional measurement.

Fixler, Gindelsky & Johnson (BEA WP2020-3) document the BEA DPI methodology and contrast a national-accounts-based personal-income distribution with tax-data (PSZ, Auten-Splinter) and Census/CPS money-income measures. Methodological proposal: anchor inequality measurement to NIPA personal income for consistency with GDP.

Methodological brief explaining differential privacy as a formal disclosure-avoidance framework: adding calibrated statistical noise to every published statistic to bound reidentification risk while preserving data utility, situated within the Bureau's long history of confidentiality protections (suppression from 1930, table/cell rules in 1970s-80s, data swapping in 1990-2010). Disclosure-avoidance method description.

Lebow-Rudd (Federal Reserve Board) survey of CPI measurement error, estimating the US CPI overstates the change in the cost of living by ~0.6 percentage point per year (confidence interval 0.1-1.2 pp). Decomposes bias into upper-level substitution (~0.1pp), lower-level substitution (~0.05pp, reduced after the BLS 1999 geometric-means formula), new-outlet (~0.05pp), a newly identified 'weighting' bias from CES-derived expenditure weights (~0.05-0.1pp), and quality-change/new-items bias (the largest and most uncertain). Estimate is below the 1996 Boskin Advisory Commission's ~1.1pp partly because of BLS procedural improvements.

Phillips-Wang (Dallas Fed WP 1608) confirm statistically significant residual seasonality in officially seasonally-adjusted US real GDP since 1990 (following Rudebusch et al. 2015). Double seasonal adjustment via X-12-ARIMA raises first-quarter growth substantially (e.g. 2016Q1 from 0.8% official to ~2.4%) but is of only moderate quality; the optimal fix is for BEA to release not-seasonally-adjusted aggregate data (which BEA announced it would do by mid-2018). Notes BEA's mid-2015 procedural changes (McCulla-Smith 2015) to reduce residual seasonality.

description: Cleveland Fed Economic Commentary (Rich-Verbrugge-Zaman) documenting that limited-influence trend-inflation estimators (median PCE, trimmed-mean PCE) are biased when the cross-sectional price-change distribution is skewed, and proposing a skewness-based bias adjustment (regression of bias on a robust Bowley/Kelly skewness measure). description: Regular periodic publication of the U.S. national index in roughly its present framework was established beginning February 1921.

Pending the full 1940 revision, BLS introduced interim methodological changes: revised weights for combining group indexes into the all-items index, revised population weights for combining cities, a complete revision of food-item weights (city-specific expenditure weights replacing regional weights), and adoption of the imputation principle for unmeasured items.

First comprehensive revision completed: new weights based on the 1934-36 expenditure study were introduced and revised indexes computed back to 1935 (partially back to 1925); the reference base period was shifted to 1935-39=100.
Reference base period shifted to 1935-39=100 on advice of the Central Statistical Board, concurrent with the 1940 comprehensive revision.
Monthly index publication inaugurated in October 1940 at the request of the National Defense Advisory Commission (replacing the quarterly indexes begun in 1935).

During World War II, following institution of rent controls, BLS switched to collecting rent data directly from tenants rather than from management; weights were reduced on rationed foods and unavailable durable items (autos, washing machines, radios) were dropped temporarily with imputed price movements.

Major changes to food-price processing: separate average prices computed for chain vs independent stores combined with fixed internal weights; food outlet samples revised by store type, sales volume and location; the costly matched-sample procedure abandoned in large cities in favor of comparing average price quotations across periods.

Interim adjustment (pending the 1953 revision): group weights adjusted using 1947-49 seven-city expenditure surveys, 25 additional items added to pricing, and 1950 population weights introduced; prompted by Korean War price shifts and escalator-clause use.

New-unit-bias correction: the rent index was raised 6.8 index points and the all-items index by 1.8 points to correct downward bias from rent control; the correction was spread back to 1940. Old-series and adjusted index published in parallel through 1952.
magnitude: rent +6.8 index points; all-items +1.8 index points

The 1953 revision made a major scope change: the purchase of a home (owned homes) was included in the weighting diagram for the first time; small urban places down to 2,500 population were added to the city sample.
Reference base period changed from 1935-39 to 1947-49 as part of the second comprehensive revision; indexes recomputed retroactively on the 1947-49 base.

description: The International Price Program (IPP) was established at BLS in 1971 to produce import and export price indexes, following 1961 NBER recommendations to the Joint Economic Committee and the Kravis-Lipsey feasibility study.
BLS published the first annual U.S. Import and Export Price Indexes in 1973.
IPP began collecting and publishing international price indexes on a quarterly basis in 1974 (up from the first annual indexes in 1973), responding to demand for more timely data.

IPP adopted a probability sampling technique (systematic probability-proportionate-to-size) for the first two sampling stages in 1976; it was extended to the subsequent stages in 1982, replacing the earlier judgmental selection of establishments and items.

In 1982 OMB placed the IPP import and export price indexes on its list of Principal Federal Economic Indicators, alongside the CPI and PPI, once full coverage of import and export goods categories was achieved.
IPP released its first price index for select services (export air passenger fares) on a quarterly basis, beginning with the first quarter of 1986.

Beginning in 1989 IPP divided the import and export merchandise universes into halves, fielding one import half and one export half each year so both universes are fully resampled every two years, with products priced about five years per sample.
Starting in 1989 BLS began producing a limited number of import/export indexes monthly, primarily to let the Census Bureau publish monthly merchandise trade statistics on an inflation-adjusted basis.

Beginning with March 1992 data, BLS began publishing import/export price indexes using harmonized-system classifications at the product level; HS historical data extend back to 1993 (versus 1974 for the older SITC system).

citation.quote: publishing price indexes using harmonized classifications

description: With the release of March 1992 data, IPP added import locality-of-origin indexes (merchandise trade classified by industrial origin for Japan, Canada, the EU, and the Asian Newly Industrialized Countries).

As of January 1997 IPP added sampling weights at the item and company levels for lowest-level stratum indexes; in prior years items were weighted equally within the detailed product category. Upper-level weights were also moved to 1995 trade values (from 1990 weights for 1993-96 data).
Beginning in 2001 BLS started providing monthly publications for select services indexes.
Annual reweighting of the import and export price indexes was introduced in 2004; previously the indexes were reweighted every five years.
In 2004 BLS began web-repricing data collection, letting survey respondents submit monthly prices electronically.

Beginning in 2005 BLS started publishing import/export price indexes using NAICS (North American Industry Classification System) classifications at the industry level, complementing the harmonized commodity and BEA end-use systems.

description: In 2005 the country and region coverage of the locality-of-origin import price indexes was expanded, adding six more countries and regions.

In 2012 the detailed industry coverage of the locality-of-origin import price indexes was expanded, adding additional industries for select countries and regions.

In 2018 BLS published, for the first time, export price indexes by locality of destination and U.S. terms-of-trade indexes by locality (retroactive to December 2017), and introduced tables comparing import price indexes with their PPI counterparts.

Starting in 2019 BLS raised the publication threshold so commodity-area indexes are published when annual import or export trade value is at least $4.76 billion (with exceptions for BEA end-use indexes important to GDP deflation).

description: Methodology note for the Aruoba-Diebold-Scotti (ADS) Business Conditions Index, a daily real-activity index produced by the Philadelphia Fed's Real-Time Data Research Center. ADS blends six mixed-frequency series (weekly initial jobless claims; monthly payrolls, industrial production, real personal income ex-transfers, real manufacturing-and-trade sales; quarterly real GDP) in a dynamic-factor/state-space model estimated by Kalman filter/smoother and ML (BFGS). Index has a theoretical mean of zero and unit variance by construction; daily estimates are produced back to 1960 and updated ~7-8 times monthly as component data are released or revised.

ADS COVID-19 treatment change: as of the 2023-09-28 vintage, COVID-era extreme component values are set to missing for parameter estimation but restored when computing the published ADS series. Prior to that vintage, COVID extremes were handled instead by truncating the estimation sample to before 2020-03-14.

During the 2025 US federal government shutdown (begun 2025-10-01) the ADS lost its federal-agency source data; the Philadelphia Fed implemented special procedures to keep updating the index from initial jobless-claims (IJC) data, with the first such update produced for 2025-10-16.
